title: Which decimal is the biggest?
hook: One has one digit after the point, one has two, one has three. Which counts for most?

doesNotKnow: how to compare decimals of different lengths

misconception: The decimal with more digits is bigger, so 0.125 > 0.25 > 0.3 ("longer is larger").
objective: The learner can explain that 0.3 > 0.25 > 0.125 because each decimal place is worth a tenth of the one before, so decimals are compared from the first digit after the point.

claims.text: 0.3 is 3 tenths, 0.25 is 2 tenths and 5 hundredths, and 0.125 is 1 tenth, 2 hundredths and 5 thousandths (stage: blocks, slivers and hairlines).
claims.source: Decimal notation: 0.3 = 3/10, 0.25 = 25/100, 0.125 = 125/1000. The stage adds digit d at place p as d pieces of width 10^-(p+1) on a 0-to-1 scale (true to scale). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Read Demo.tsx first. NUMS digits [3], [2,5], [1,2,5]. Each press draws d pieces of width SCALE/10^(p+1), so the bars are 3 blocks; 2 blocks and 5 slivers; 1 block, 2 slivers and 5 hairlines. Own port of the drawn widths: 74.4, 62.0 and 31.0 px of 248, i.e. 0.300, 0.250 and 0.125.

claims.text: 0.3 is the largest of the three and its bar is the longest: 0.3 > 0.25 > 0.125 (300 > 250 > 125 thousandths).
claims.source: Convert to thousandths. node: [0.3, 0.25, 0.125].sort((a,b)=>a-b) = [0.125, 0.25, 0.3]. The stage computes values in integer thousandths (thousandths()) and the reveal names the largest from that sort. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own port: thousandths() full values 300, 250, 125, sorted 0.3 > 0.25 > 0.125. The reveal's largest = NUMS[order[0]].label = '0.3'. The bar widths are to scale (74.4 > 62.0 > 31.0 px), so the longest bar is 0.3 once all are built, and 'built' requires all of them built.

claims.text: The five hundredth-slivers of 0.25 add 0.05, which is less than the one more tenth-block (0.1) it would need to reach 0.3.
claims.source: 5 × 0.01 = 0.05 < 0.1; 0.2 + 0.05 = 0.25 < 0.3. node check. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. The reveal prints show(b25h × 10) = show(50) = '0.05'. 0.25 has 2 tenth-blocks against 0.3's 3, so it is one block (0.1) short at the tenths place, and its 5 slivers add 0.05 < 0.1. Arithmetic checked in node.

claims.text: Each decimal place is worth one tenth of the place to its left, so extra digits only add smaller and smaller pieces; compare decimals from the first digit after the point.
claims.source: Place value definition: the k-th place after the point is worth 10^-k. Because any digits after place k add less than one unit of place k (at most 0.0999… of it), the first differing digit decides. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Place value: 10^−(p+1) per place, each a tenth of the one to its left. That is the definition of decimal notation (convention), drawn on stage as width SCALE/10^(p+1). Comparing from the first digit after the point is valid here because every number has integer part 0, and the reveal says it in that context.

claims.text: Stage legend: a block is 0.1, a sliver is 0.01 and a hairline is 0.001.
claims.source: Definition of the stage pieces (widths SCALE/10, SCALE/100, SCALE/1000 in Demo.tsx). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Caption after the prediction: 'Block = 0.1 · sliver = 0.01 · hairline = 0.001', exact. The CSS classes are tenth, hundredth and thousandth, with widths 24.8, 2.48 and 0.248 px on the 248 px scale.

recall.question: Which is larger: 0.4 or 0.375?
recall.why: Compare from the first digit after the point: 4 tenths beat 3 tenths. The 75 thousandths of 0.375 add less than one more tenth.
